items.name: Software engineering (IEEE): systematic, disciplined, quantifiable
items.memorize: Applying a systematic, disciplined and quantifiable approach to the development, operation and maintenance of software

items.name: Software engineering phases
items.memorize: Requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance

items.name: Problem-solving states: initial, operational, goal
items.memorize: Initial (interpret the problem) · Operational (think up viable solutions) · Goal (solution identified, evaluated and validated)

items.name: Functional fixedness
items.memorize: Seeing objects only in their usual function, which blocks solutions. The 9-dots puzzle: lines don't have to start and end on a dot

items.name: Holistic problem-solving framework (6 tasks)
items.memorize: Interpret the problem · evaluate constraints · collaborative brainstorming · synthesize the possibilities · evaluate the solution · implement it

items.name: Design as a process vs as a product
items.memorize: Process: activities to model structure and behavior before construction (project management) · Product: the artifacts such as class diagrams (technical)

items.name: Why study design: project management vs technical reasons
items.memorize: PM: minimizes requirements volatility, efficient staffing, no "one guy" owning the system · Technical: maps requirements to models, identifies components, evaluates quality, reuse, foundation for all later work

items.name: Five software design challenges
items.memorize: Requirements volatility · inconsistent development processes · fast, ever-changing technology · managing design influences (stakeholders) · ethical and professional practices

items.name: Design process: major and supporting activities
items.memorize: Major: software architecture, detailed design · Supporting: construction design, human-computer interface design, design documentation, management activities

items.name: Architecture (black-box, non-functional) vs detailed design (white-box, functional)
items.memorize: Architecture: macro-design, black-box models, major components, mostly quality requirements · Detailed design: internals of components, white-box, mostly functional requirements

items.name: Component design vs interface design (internal and external interfaces)
Designer roles
items.memorize: Systems engineer (whole system, hardware + software) · software architect (black-box, quality) · component designer (internals, codes them) · UI designer (usability)

items.name: Eight design principles
items.memorize: Modularization · abstraction · encapsulation · coupling · cohesion · separation of interface and implementation · completeness · sufficiency

items.name: Modularization and its advantages
items.memorize: Continuous decomposition into fine-grained components · keeps complexity manageable, isolates errors, removes redundancy, encourages reuse

items.name: Abstraction: functional (procedural) vs data
items.memorize: Focus on essential characteristics, defer details. Modularization says what to separate, abstraction says how. Functional: SEND · Data: MESSAGE

items.name: Encapsulation vs abstraction
items.memorize: Abstraction hides what is not needed; encapsulation enforces that only essential information is exposed (private fields, public methods)

items.name: Coupling types, worst to best
items.memorize: Content (modifies another module's internals) · common (global variables) · external (shared format, protocol or device) · control (passes a what-to-do flag) · stamp (passes a whole record, uses part) · data (parameters) · no coupling. Aim low

items.name: Cohesion types
items.memorize: Functional (one function) · procedural/sequential (steps in order) · temporal (same time) · communication (same data). Aim high

items.name: Separation of interface and implementation vs encapsulation
items.memorize: Encapsulation hides the implementation; separation lets different implementations sit behind one stable interface

items.name: Completeness vs sufficiency
items.memorize: Completeness: provides every required service (no less) · Sufficiency: only the services needed (no more)

items.name: Object-oriented vs structured (functional) design strategy
items.memorize: OO: objects with identity, state, behavior; inheritance and polymorphism · Structured: top-down functional decomposition, not for OO languages

items.name: Design considerations
items.memorize: Design for minimizing complexity · design for change

items.name: Formal definition of software architecture and its five parts
items.memorize: Foundational design (forward engineering, where quality starts) · translates requirements (text to graphics, traceable) · a collection of design elements (no single diagram) · major components with their provided quality · supports detailed design and construction

items.name: Architecture is / is not
items.memorize: Is: communication, what parts, how they fit (structure, behavior, non-functional requirements) · Is not: development, algorithms, data structures

items.name: Seven key tasks in architectural design
items.memorize: Stakeholder concerns · architectural views · styles and patterns · organizational influences · major components and interfaces · evaluate and validate · policies for design synchronicity

items.name: Nine quality attributes and their one-line definitions
items.memorize: Usability, modifiability, security, performance, reliability, portability, testability, availability (uptime), interoperability

items.name: Tactics: design decisions that achieve a quality attribute
items.memorize: Quality attribute = the goal · tactic = the design decision that controls its response (e.g. caching for performance)

items.name: Design synchronicity
items.memorize: How well the implementation reflects the architecture and detailed design. Keep it high with a defined process, including maintenance

items.name: Software architecture process (5 tasks)
items.memorize: Understand and evaluate requirements · design · evaluate · document · monitor and control implementation

items.name: Requirements engineering: elicitation, analysis, specification, validation
items.memorize: Elicitation techniques: interviews, facilitated meetings, observation, scenarios · Analysis: classification, prioritization, negotiation, conceptual modeling

items.name: Requirement classification
items.memorize: Functional vs non-functional · product vs process · imposed (by stakeholders) vs derived (by the team)

items.name: Six characteristics of good requirements
items.memorize: Specific (clear, concise, exclusive) · correct · complete · consistent · attainable · verifiable

items.name: 4+1 view model: each view, its stakeholders and UML diagrams
items.memorize: Logical: end users, analysts, designers · class, object, sequence, communication, state · Process: developers, integrators · activity, interaction overview · Development: programmers, PMs · package, component · Physical: installers, admins, system engineers · deployment · User/scenario (+1): use case, validates the other four

items.name: Pick the right UML diagram for each view
Functional requirements vs quality attributes
items.memorize: Functional: what the system shall do, planned in detailed design · Quality attributes: how well, judged on the system as a whole, planned in the architecture

items.name: Write a quality attribute scenario (all six parts)
items.memorize: Source · stimulus · environment · artifact · response · response measure. "Some source generates a stimulus that arrives at an artifact under some environment and must be dealt with by a response, measured by a response measure"

items.name: Why scenarios: overlapping and unstable QA definitions
items.memorize: A DoS attack touches availability, performance, security and usability at once, so concrete scenarios pin down what is meant

items.name: Seven categories of quality design decisions
items.memorize: Allocation of responsibilities · coordination model · data model · management of resources · mapping among elements · binding time · choice of technology

items.name: Availability tactics
items.memorize: Fault detection: ping/echo, heartbeat, exception · Recovery preparation: voting, active and passive redundancy, spare · Reintroduction: shadow, resynchronization, rollback · Prevention: removal from service, transactions, process monitor

items.name: Modifiability tactics
items.memorize: Localize changes · prevent ripple effects · defer binding time (decide at runtime, e.g. config files)

items.name: Performance: stimuli, measures and tactics
items.memorize: Stimuli: periodic, sporadic, bursty, stochastic · Measures: latency, deadline, throughput, jitter, miss rate, data loss · Tactics: resource demand, management, arbitration

items.name: Security tactics
items.memorize: Resist attacks (authenticate, authorize, confidentiality, integrity, limit exposure and access) · detect attacks (intrusion detection) · recover (restoration, audit trail)

items.name: Testability tactics
items.memorize: Manage input/output (record/playback, separate interface from implementation) · internal monitoring (built-in monitors)

items.name: Usability tactics
items.memorize: Separate the user interface · support user initiative (cancel, undo, aggregate) · support system initiative (user, system and task models)

items.name: Architectural style vs pattern vs design pattern
items.memorize: Style: overall template (layered) · architectural pattern: system-wide reusable solution (MVC) · design pattern: medium-scale, affects a subsystem

items.name: History: Alexander, 1990s styles, GoF, Buschmann
items.memorize: 1977 Alexander: 253 building patterns · 1990s: architectural styles · 1994 GoF: 23 design patterns · 1996 Buschmann et al.: architectural patterns (context, problem, solution)

items.name: Five system types and their patterns
items.memorize: Data-centered: blackboard, repository · Data flow: pipes-and-filters · Distributed: client-server, broker · Interactive: MVC · Hierarchical: layered, main program and subroutine

items.name: Blackboard pattern: components, flow and diagrams
items.memorize: Blackboard (shared data, provides read/write interface) · agents (independent solvers, provide run interface) · controller (schedules agents). Opportunistic, no fixed order; expert systems, speech and image recognition

items.name: Pipes-and-filters pattern
items.memorize: Data source → pipes → filters → data sink. Compiler (lexer → parser → code generator → optimizer), face recognition. Extensible, efficient (parallel), reusable, modifiable

items.name: Client-server pattern and its coupling problem
items.memorize: Interoperability, modifiability, availability, reusability · but clients are tightly coupled to servers

items.name: Broker pattern: client proxy, broker, server proxy, bridge
items.memorize: Mediates between clients and servers so one client reaches many servers transparently · loosely coupled · interoperability, modifiability, portability, reusability

items.name: Model-View-Controller
items.memorize: Controller takes input → model updates data → model notifies views (observer) → view shows it. Modifiability, usability, reusability

items.name: Layered pattern
items.memorize: Modifiability, portability, security, reusability

items.name: Quality properties each pattern gives
items.memorize: Pipes-and-filters: extensibility, efficiency, reusability, modifiability, security, maintainability · client-server: interoperability, modifiability, availability, reusability · broker: interoperability, modifiability, portability, reusability · MVC: modifiability, usability, reusability · layered: modifiability, portability, security, reusability

items.name: Match a scenario to its architectural pattern and draw the component diagram
Detailed design: definition and where it fits
items.memorize: Refines the architecture until it is complete enough to implement. Architecture bridges requirements and design; detailed design bridges design and code

items.name: Five key tasks in detailed design
items.memorize: Understand architecture and requirements · create detailed designs · evaluate them (technical reviews) · document them · monitor and control implementation

items.name: What creating detailed designs focuses on
items.memorize: Interface design (internal and external) · GUI design · internal component design (structural and behavioral) · data design (database, data dictionary)

items.name: Technical review guidelines
items.memorize: Send the notice early · include a technical expert, stakeholders and QA/testing · focus on how functional and non-functional requirements are met · document it and assign action items

items.name: Design documents: SDD, interface control, version control
Abstract class vs interface
items.memorize: Abstract class: at least one abstract method, can have concrete ones, cannot be instantiated, "extends" · interface: only abstract methods and constants, "implements", many per class, loose coupling

items.name: SOLID principles
items.memorize: Single responsibility · open-closed · Liskov substitution · interface segregation · dependency inversion

items.name: Single Responsibility: spot the violation and split the class
items.memorize: A module is responsible to one, and only one, actor. One reason to change. Person shouldn't validate email

items.name: Open-Closed: open to extension, closed to modification
items.memorize: Add new code instead of changing working code. GameEngine depending on a concrete character violates it; depend on an abstraction and use polymorphism

items.name: Liskov Substitution: signature and methods rules
items.memorize: Subtypes must be usable wherever the base is expected. Preconditions can only weaken, postconditions only strengthen. Square/Rectangle and Penguin/Bird violate it; License fees obey it

items.name: Interface Segregation
items.memorize: No class should depend on methods it doesn't use. Many client-specific interfaces beat one general one (roam, fly, swim)

items.name: Dependency Inversion
items.memorize: High-level modules depend on abstractions, not low-level details. Manager depends on IWorker, not Worker

items.name: Rules of design
items.memorize: Well-defined problem · what before how · separate orthogonal concerns · external before internal · keep it simple · multiple levels of abstraction · design for extensibility · rapid prototyping · details depend on abstractions · common closure · reuse together · depend toward stability · stable means abstract

items.name: Common design mistakes
items.memorize: Depth-first design · directly refining the requirements spec · ignoring potential changes · making the design too detailed

items.name: Design pattern classification: purpose and scope
items.memorize: Purpose: creational (creating objects), structural (composing structures), behavioral (interaction and responsibility) · Scope: class (design time) vs object (run time)

items.name: Abstract Factory: families of related products
items.memorize: Interface for creating families of related objects without naming concrete classes. 7 steps: product interfaces, families, concrete products, factory interface, concrete factories, associate, client. Pros: consistency, OCP. Con: many classes

items.name: Factory Method: let subclasses decide what to instantiate
items.memorize: One creation method in the creator; concrete creators return concrete products (ComputerStore → StandardComputerStore). One product type with many implementations

items.name: Builder: same steps, different representations
items.memorize: Director runs the steps, builder interface declares them, concrete builders implement them, product is the result. One complex object step by step (code generator, burgers, sandwiches)

items.name: Singleton: one instance, global access (diagram and code)
items.memorize: Private constructor · private static instance · public static getInstance(). Event manager/logger. Drawback: multithreading

items.name: Prototype: copy existing objects with clone()
Abstract Factory vs Factory Method vs Builder
items.memorize: Factory method: one product type · abstract factory: whole families at once · builder: one complex object, built in steps at discrete times

items.name: Adapter: object vs class adapter
items.memorize: Converts one interface into the one clients expect (BirdAdapter makes a Sparrow act as a ToyDuck). Object adapter uses composition and is preferred; class adapter needs multiple inheritance

items.name: Composite: tree of whole-part objects treated uniformly
items.memorize: Component base · leaf · composite holds children and adds/removes them. File system: folder size sums its children

items.name: Facade: one simple interface to a complex subsystem
items.memorize: ShopKeeper in front of the mobile shop subsystem. Hides internals, stable interface, weak coupling

items.name: Iterator: traverse a collection without knowing its representation
items.memorize: Iterator interface (hasNext, next) · aggregate with createIterator(). Supports different traversals

items.name: Observer: one-to-many notification
items.memorize: Subject attach/detach/notify · observers implement update(). Weather station and dashboards, influencer and followers

items.name: Step-by-step recipe for applying each pattern
Benefits of architecture evaluation
items.memorize: Prioritizes conflicting goals · forces a clear explanation · improves documentation · uncovers cross-project reuse · improves architecture practices

items.name: ATAM, SAAM and ARID (common point: scenarios and quality attributes)
items.memorize: Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method · Software Architecture Analysis Method · Active Reviews for Intermediate Designs. All use scenarios and quality attributes

items.name: Quality attribute perspectives
items.memorize: End user: performance, availability, usability, security · technical: modifiability, portability, reusability, testability, interoperability · business: time to market, cost and benefit, lifetime, budget

items.name: ATAM participants and team roles
items.memorize: Evaluation team (3–5 architects), project decision makers, architecture stakeholders · roles: team leader, evaluation leader, scenario scribe, proceedings scribe, questioner

items.name: ATAM nine steps
items.memorize: Present ATAM · business drivers · architecture · identify approaches · utility tree · analyze approaches · brainstorm and prioritize scenarios · analyze again · present results

items.name: Quality attribute utility tree
items.memorize: Top-down: quality goals as high-level nodes, scenarios as leaves rated by importance and difficulty

items.name: ATAM output and risks, non-risks, sensitivity points, trade-offs
ATAM vs lightweight ATAM
items.memorize: Lightweight: smaller, less risky projects, half a day to a day, internal participants only, less depth and objectivity

items.name: Why document, and the three uses of documentation
items.memorize: Education · communication among stakeholders · analysis of quality attributes

items.name: Starting documentation
items.memorize: Select views · define stakeholders · identify their concerns · decide what and how to document (templates)

items.name: View sets: 4+1, Siemens four views, Herzum & Sims, Software Cost Reduction
items.memorize: Siemens: conceptual, module interconnection, execution, code · SCR: module, process, uses

items.name: Templates and the minimum information to document
items.memorize: RUP template · SEI (Views and Beyond) template · minimum: problem description, context, rationale, principles and guidelines, structure, views, quality attributes

items.name: Documenting a view (5 parts)
items.memorize: Primary presentation · element catalog · context diagram · variability guide · architecture background

items.name: Documentation beyond views (6 parts)
items.memorize: Documentation roadmap · view documentation · system overview · mapping between views · rationale · directory
